Rust has three nested words for "code organisation" and they are easy to confuse. Get them straight once:

Word Means Example
Module a namespace inside a crate mod db;
Crate one compilation unit — a library or a binary myapp, serde
Package a Cargo.toml with one or more crates the folder myapp/

A package has at most one library crate plus any number of binary crates. All of them can share modules.

Modules

Visibility

Modifier Visible to
(nothing) the current module and its children
pub everyone
pub(crate) the whole crate, not external users
pub(super) the parent module
pub(in crate::api) that specific path

Rule of thumb: default to private, then pub(crate) for internal sharing, then pub only for what is genuinely part of your API. Public API is a promise you have to keep.

The module tree

pub use is the facade pattern: internal structure can change freely while the public path stays stable.

Paths: crate, self, super

use and aliasing

Group order convention (rustfmt enforces within a group):

Gotcha: use is not a copy or an import at runtime — it only brings a name into scope. use at the top of a function body is legal and useful for long paths inside one function.

Glob imports

Use for #[cfg(test)] mod tests { use super::*; } (standard) and for crate preludes. Avoid in production modules — you lose track of where names come from and unused-import warnings.

Crates

A crate is what rustc compiles. It has a root file:

Crate kind Root Produces
library src/lib.rs .rlib, .so/.dll
binary src/main.rs an executable

Any .rs file in src/bin/ is automatically a binary. That is the quickest way to add a helper tool:

Crate names and use names

Cargo package names use hyphens (my-app), but Rust crate names use underscores (my_app). Cargo converts automatically; in code you always write the underscore form.

extern crate is dead

Since the 2018 edition, dependencies are in scope automatically. Delete any extern crate you find except in specific macro/no_std situations.

Re-exports: building a clean public API

Callers now write myapp::User and myapp::Result regardless of how the internals are arranged. Renaming a module becomes a non-breaking change.

Conditional compilation

Test the matrix:

Gotcha: cfg blocks that do not compile are never checked by default. A Windows-only module can rot for months. Add --all-targets and a cross-target cargo check to CI.

Documentation as part of the module system

  • //! documents the containing item (module or crate).
  • /// documents the following item.
  • #[doc(hidden)] hides an item from the docs but keeps it public.
  • #[doc = include_str!("../README.md")] puts your README on the crate page.

A worked example: a multi-binary package

Exercises

  1. Split a single-file program into lib.rs + main.rs, with a store module containing two implementations behind a pub trait.
  2. Add pub use re-exports so external code writes myapp::Store, not myapp::store::memory::MemoryStore.
  3. Add a second binary in src/bin/ that reuses the library.
  4. Add a #[cfg(feature = "extra")] module and verify cargo check fails to see it without the feature, and passes with it.
  5. Write crate-level //! docs and run cargo doc --open. Confirm your doc example is executed by cargo test.
